t: Minimize OR of Remaining Elements Using Operations
o: Each operation replaces two adjacent elements by their AND (up to k times); minimize the OR of what remains. A target OR bit b can be turned off only if every surviving element lacks bit b, i.e., the array partitions into maximal AND-runs each lacking b, costing (run length − 1) merges. Process bits from high to low, greedily committing cleared bits: example 2 clears bit 1 (value 2) with 4 ops leaving OR = 2.
k: Bit b is clearable iff the array splits into runs whose AND lacks b (and lacks all previously committed cleared bits), using ≤ k merges.
Greedy high→low: commit clearing bit b when feasible; otherwise it stays in the answer.

a.n: Approach 1: Greedy bit descent with feasibility scan
a.i: Maintain mask `fixed` of bits already forced to 0 in every final element. For candidate bit b (high→low), scan the array accumulating AND-runs; a run must keep merging until its AND has neither bit b nor any fixed bit. Total merges needed must be ≤ k and the final run must satisfy the condition; if so, add b to fixed, else set b in the answer. Higher bits are prioritized correctly because clearing them is always at least as valuable.
s: For b from 29 down to 0: simulate runs, counting merges until each run's AND clears b and all fixed bits.
If feasible within k merges, fixed |= 1<<b; else ans |= 1<<b.

w: The key correctness point: once we decide to clear a set of bits, every surviving element must lack ALL of them, hence the `fixed` mask inside the run condition. Pitfalls: ops counts merges (runs of length L cost L−1; the loop above counts one per consumed element, which equals merges within each run), and the trailing partial run must also be validated. Follow-up: prove the greedy bit priority is optimal via an exchange argument on OR values.
